learning_goal: Name the four bony pillars and the roof of the carpal tunnel, list the ten things inside it, name the things that pass outside it, and explain from that list why carpal tunnel syndrome numbs the fingers but spares the palm.

structures.name: flexor retinaculum of right wrist
structures.label: Flexor retinaculum
structures.narration: A thick band, about two centimetres square, stretched across the front of the carpal arch. It is the roof and it does not stretch — which is the whole problem in carpal tunnel syndrome, and the reason the treatment is to cut it.

structures.name: right scaphoid
structures.label: Scaphoid
structures.narration: Its tubercle is the upper lateral post the retinaculum is tied to. You feel it at the base of the thenar eminence when the wrist is bent back.

structures.name: right trapezium
structures.label: Trapezium
structures.narration: The lower lateral post. Its tubercle has a groove beside it, and flexor carpi radialis runs in that groove — inside the retinaculum's grip but outside the tunnel proper.

structures.name: right pisiform
structures.label: Pisiform
structures.narration: The upper medial post. A pea-sized sesamoid sitting in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris — the easiest carpal bone to feel on yourself.

structures.name: right hamate
structures.label: Hamate
structures.narration: The lower medial post. Its hook is the ridge you press on beyond the pisiform; the ulnar nerve passes between the two, in Guyon's canal, on top of the retinaculum and outside the tunnel.

structures.name: right lunate
structures.label: Lunate
structures.narration: Part of the floor. A dislocated lunate falls forwards into the tunnel and squeezes the median nerve acutely — the one presentation of these symptoms that is an emergency.

structures.name: right capitate
structures.label: Capitate
structures.narration: The largest carpal bone, at the keystone of the arch. The floor is a curve, not a plate — the bones themselves make the hollow.

structures.name: right triquetral
structures.label: Triquetral
structures.narration: Sits behind the pisiform in the proximal row and completes the medial side of the floor.

structures.name: right trapezoid
structures.label: Trapezoid
structures.narration: The small bone between trapezium and capitate, deep in the floor of the arch.

structures.label: Tubercle of the scaphoid
structures.calibrated_by: contact: nearest point on the right scaphoid (FMA24435, 23.8 mm span, right side, long axis x) to the flexor retinaculum (FMA40120). Gap 0.45 mm — the surfaces meet. One witness.
terms: proximal lateral attachment of the flexor retinaculum
structures.narration: The proximal lateral post. Measured here as the point where the scaphoid actually touches the retinaculum, not by eye.

structures.label: Tubercle of the trapezium
structures.calibrated_by: contact: nearest point on the right trapezium (FMA24443, 20.1 mm span, right side, long axis z) to the flexor retinaculum (FMA40120). Gap 0.20 mm — the tightest of the four attachments. One witness.
terms: distal lateral attachment of the flexor retinaculum
structures.narration: The distal lateral post. The groove for flexor carpi radialis lies immediately medial to it.

structures.label: Hook of the hamate
structures.calibrated_by: contact: nearest point on the right hamate (FMA24448, 22.8 mm span, right side, long axis y) to the flexor retinaculum (FMA40120). Gap 2.80 mm — the loosest of the three measured, within the 3 mm tolerance but the one to re-check first. One witness.
terms: distal medial attachment of the flexor retinaculum
structures.narration: The distal medial post, and the lateral wall of Guyon's canal. It is the carpal bone that breaks in a golfer or a batsman gripping a handle.

structures.name: humeroulnar head of right flexor digitorum superficialis
structures.label: Flexor digitorum superficialis — humeroulnar head
structures.narration: Four tendons enter the tunnel from this muscle. In the tunnel they lie in two pairs — middle and ring in front, index and little behind — inside one common flexor sheath.

structures.name: radial head of right flexor digitorum superficialis
structures.label: Flexor digitorum superficialis — radial head
terms: radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis
structures.narration: The second head of the same muscle. Its tendons join the same four.

structures.name: right flexor digitorum profundus
structures.label: Flexor digitorum profundus
structures.narration: Four more tendons, lying flat on the floor of the tunnel behind the superficialis pairs.

structures.name: right flexor pollicis longus
structures.label: Flexor pollicis longus
structures.narration: The ninth tendon, most lateral, in its own sheath. Four plus four plus one is nine tendons — and the median nerve makes ten structures in the tunnel.

structures.name: right abductor pollicis brevis
structures.label: Abductor pollicis brevis
structures.narration: The muscle you test for a median nerve lesion: ask the patient to lift the thumb straight off the table against your finger. It arises partly from the retinaculum it sits on.

structures.name: right opponens pollicis
structures.label: Opponens pollicis
structures.narration: Swings the thumb across the palm to meet the fingers. Lose it and the hand can no longer grip anything round.

structures.name: superficial head of right flexor pollicis brevis
structures.label: Flexor pollicis brevis — superficial head
structures.narration: The third thenar muscle supplied by the median nerve. All three waste together, and the thenar eminence flattens.

structures.name: deep head of right flexor pollicis brevis
structures.label: Flexor pollicis brevis — deep head
terms: deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
structures.narration: The exception: this head is usually ulnar. It is why a little thumb flexion survives even a complete median nerve lesion.

structures.name: right palmaris longus
structures.label: Palmaris longus
structures.narration: Runs over the roof, not under it, and blends into the palmar aponeurosis. The median nerve lies just deep and lateral to it — which is exactly why a careless cut at the wrist finds the nerve.

structures.name: right flexor carpi radialis
structures.label: Flexor carpi radialis
structures.narration: Slips into its own groove in the trapezium, in a split layer of the retinaculum. Examiners like this one: it is under the retinaculum but never in the tunnel.

structures.name: ulnar head of right flexor carpi ulnaris
structures.label: Flexor carpi ulnaris — ulnar head
structures.narration: Stops at the pisiform and never enters the tunnel. It is the tendon that leads your thumb to the pisiform, and the pisiform that leads you to Guyon's canal.

structures.name: right radius
structures.label: Radius
structures.narration: The tunnel begins where the radius ends. A badly healed Colles fracture is one of the classic causes of a tunnel that has become too small.

structures.name: right ulna
structures.label: Ulna
structures.narration: Sits medial and stops short of the carpus.

structures.name: right first metacarpal bone
structures.label: First metacarpal
structures.narration: The thumb ray. The thenar muscles run from the retinaculum to its base.

structures.name: right third metacarpal bone
structures.label: Third metacarpal
structures.narration: The middle ray, straight ahead of the tunnel's mouth — the line the long flexor tendons take into the palm.

structures.name: right fifth metacarpal bone
structures.label: Fifth metacarpal
structures.narration: The little finger ray, on the ulnar side — the territory the ulnar nerve keeps even when the median nerve is dead.

views.title: Where the tunnel is
views.narration: The carpal tunnel is the space between the front of the wrist bones and the band stretched across them. Everything that has to reach the palm from the front of the forearm either goes through it or squeezes past it.

views.title: The floor is an arch
views.narration: Eight carpal bones, two rows of four, and they do not lie flat. The row curls forwards at each end, so the bones alone already make a gutter. The tunnel is that gutter with a lid on it.

views.title: Four pillars
views.narration: The retinaculum is tied to four bony points, marked here on the bones. Laterally the tubercle of the scaphoid and the tubercle of the trapezium; medially the pisiform — a whole bone, so no marker is needed — and the hook of the hamate. Proximal pair first, distal pair second — that is the order to recite them in.

views.title: Put the lid on
views.narration: The retinaculum bridges the four pillars and turns the gutter into a closed tunnel. Bone on three sides, a ligament on the fourth: nothing here can give way when the contents swell.

views.title: Cut across the tunnel
views.narration: This is the section every exam draws. Roof in front, carpal arch behind, and inside: the four superficialis tendons in two pairs, the four profundus tendons flat on the floor, flexor pollicis longus on the lateral side, and the median nerve pressed up against the roof.

views.title: Nine tendons
views.narration: Count them: four from superficialis, four from profundus, one from flexor pollicis longus. Nine tendons and one nerve. Nothing else belongs in here — no artery, no vein of consequence, and no other nerve.

views.title: The tenth structure
views.narration: The path traced here is the median nerve. It comes down the forearm behind flexor digitorum superficialis, enters the tunnel under the retinaculum with the nine tendons, and gives off its recurrent branch to the thenar muscles the moment it emerges. That branch is a few millimetres from the skin of the palm — the reason a wrist laceration can cost a thumb its opposition.

views.title: What passes outside
views.narration: Four things pass the wrist without entering the tunnel. Palmaris longus over the roof. Flexor carpi radialis in its own groove in the trapezium. Flexor carpi ulnaris stopping at the pisiform. And the ulnar nerve and artery in Guyon's canal, on top of the retinaculum between pisiform and hook of hamate. That is why carpal tunnel syndrome never affects the little finger.

views.title: Take the roof off
views.narration: Cutting the retinaculum is the operation. The tunnel opens, the pressure falls, and nothing important is lost — the band's only job is to stop the tendons bowstringing forwards when you grip.

views.title: Why the palm is spared
views.narration: Two findings follow from the anatomy. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve above the wrist and crosses over the retinaculum, so the skin of the palm keeps its sensation while the fingers go numb — that sign separates a tunnel from a lesion higher up. And of the thenar muscles only the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis is ulnar, so in a long-standing case the eminence flattens but weak thumb flexion remains.

gaps: There is no median nerve mesh in the catalog — no peripheral nerve of the upper limb has one — so the single most important content of the carpal tunnel is authored as a traced concept path with narration, not as a model. The same applies to the ulnar nerve and artery in Guyon's canal, the recurrent and palmar cutaneous branches, and the superficial palmar arch.

RESOLVED 2026-08-29: this note previously said the carpal meshes were not in the local mesh set, so no attachment landmark could be measured. That was stale — all twenty-five of this scene's models are present. The retinaculum is tied to FOUR points, of which the pisiform is a whole bone and needs no marker; the other three are now measured landmark anchors, derived as the nearest point on each bone to the flexor retinaculum: scaphoid tubercle 0.45 mm, trapezium tubercle 0.20 mm, hook of hamate 2.80 mm. Each has one witness only, and all three are status needs-review until a human clears them in-app.

There is no mesh for the common flexor synovial sheath, the radial bursa, the palmar aponeurosis or the transverse carpal ligament as a structure separate from the flexor retinaculum, so the sheaths the tendons run in are described rather than shown.

Tendons are not modelled separately from their muscle bellies: a scene that says "nine tendons in the tunnel" is showing four muscles whose tendons those are. The count is taught in narration and in the cross-section beat.

The scaphoid, lunate, capitate, triquetral and trapezoid also appear in the wrist beats of the Radius & ulna scene. That is deliberate overlap — this scene is the one that teaches them as the wall of a tunnel.
